title: WhatsApp-First Customer Experience: Why GCC Brands Are Ditching Traditional Helpdesks
subtitle: Customer expectations in Dubai, Riyadh, and Doha demand immediate, bilingual conversational commerce and support rather than ticket queues.
excerpt: Analysis of how regional retail, travel, and healthcare companies achieve 4x higher resolution rates by embedding WhatsApp Business API natively into their CRM stacks.
imageCaption: Bilingual customer service team in Dubai managing unified conversational pipelines over WhatsApp.
keyTakeaways: WhatsApp is the primary business communication medium in the GCC with over 93% smartphone penetration.
Traditional email helpdesk tickets suffer from low response rates compared to WhatsApp conversational flows.
Modern customer support suites like Freshdesk and HubSpot now offer deep WhatsApp Business API integration.
content: In the Middle East, the traditional customer support ticket submitted via email is rapidly becoming an obsolete artifact of the past.

Consumer and corporate behavior in the UAE and Saudi Arabia is deeply rooted in real-time messaging. High-net-worth real estate buyers, fintech users, and e-commerce shoppers expect immediate, personalized dialogue over WhatsApp rather than waiting for an automated email receipt.

Leading regional brands that have unified their CRM pipelines with the official WhatsApp Business API report a 70% reduction in first-response times and a dramatic improvement in customer satisfaction scores.

title: ZATCA Phase 2 E-Invoicing Expansion: Mid-Market ERP Selection Playbook for 2026
subtitle: A detailed breakdown of certified ERP and accounting platforms that support cryptographic stamps, XML syntax, and direct Fatoora integration.
excerpt: With ZATCA Phase 2 rolling out to mid-tier commercial enterprises in Saudi Arabia, choosing the right accounting software has become an existential compliance priority.

author.name: Tariq Al-Mansoor
author.role: Head of Regional ERP & AI Research

imageCaption: Tax compliance specialist verifying ZATCA Phase 2 cryptographic invoice hashes in Riyadh.
keyTakeaways: ZATCA Phase 2 requires real-time cryptographic stamp identifiers (CSID) and XML transmission.
Zoho Books and Odoo ERP provide official out-of-the-box certification without third-party middleware.
Companies failing to integrate certified systems face strict penalties and invoice rejection.
content: Saudi Arabia's Fatoora e-invoicing initiative under the Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (ZATCA) represents one of the most comprehensive digital tax rollouts in global history.

In Phase 2, businesses cannot merely issue PDF receipts with static QR codes. Every commercial invoice must be generated in standardized UBL 2.1 XML syntax, cryptographically signed with a private key, and transmitted to the ZATCA portal in real-time.

Mid-market enterprises that attempt to bridge legacy accounting systems with external middleware frequently encounter synchronization failures. We evaluate why native certified ERP modules—such as Zoho Books and Odoo—offer the safest path to sustained regulatory compliance.

title: Saudi Contact Centres Put Arabic Speech AI Through Dialect Tests Before Signing
subtitle: Buyers in Riyadh and Jeddah are running their own recorded-call trials to see whether transcription and summarisation tools cope with Najdi, Hejazi and mixed Arabic-English speech.
excerpt: Voice AI demos sound convincing in a meeting room. Saudi customer service leaders are increasingly asking vendors to prove accuracy on their own calls before any contract is signed.

author.name: Tariq Al-Mansoor
author.role: Head of Regional ERP & AI Research

imageCaption: A green paper speech bubble beside crumpled yellow paper on a yellow background.
keyTakeaways: Saudi buyers are moving from vendor demos to structured trials on their own anonymised call recordings.
Dialect coverage, code-switching between Arabic and English, and handling of names and numbers are the most common failure points.
Any trial using real customer calls needs a PDPL-compliant basis and clear data-handling terms with the vendor.
content: Speech analytics and AI call summaries have become a standard line item in contact centre software proposals across the Kingdom. What has changed over the past year, according to customer service leaders we spoke to in Riyadh and Jeddah, is how those features are evaluated. Rather than accepting a polished demo recorded in Modern Standard Arabic, more buyers are insisting on a structured trial using a sample of their own calls, scored against human-checked transcripts.

The reason is practical. A typical call into a Saudi bank, telecom operator or retailer rarely stays in one register. Customers move between Najdi or Hejazi Arabic, Modern Standard Arabic and English within a single sentence, and read out account numbers, Hijri dates and product names that generic models often mishandle. A summary that misreads a single figure can send an agent down the wrong path or create a compliance problem later.

Several heads of customer experience told us they now ask vendors for accuracy results broken down by dialect and by call type, not a single headline number. They also look at how the tool handles silence, hold music and agents speaking over customers, all of which are common in real recordings and absent from demos. Some also ask for results on a second sample a month later, to see whether accuracy holds once the novelty of the trial has passed.

subheadings.title: How buyers are structuring trials
paragraphs: The trials we heard about follow a similar pattern. A team selects a few hundred calls across its main queues, removes or masks personal details, and has a small group of native-speaking reviewers produce reference transcripts. Each shortlisted vendor processes the same set, and results are compared on word accuracy, correct capture of numbers and names, and whether the generated summary would let a second agent pick up the case without listening to the call.

subheadings.title: The data protection question
paragraphs: Because call recordings contain personal data, Saudi buyers are treating these trials as processing activities under the Personal Data Protection Law rather than informal tests. That means agreeing where the audio will be processed and stored, how long the vendor may keep it, and whether it can be used to train models. Several buyers said they now reject trials outright where a vendor cannot answer those questions in writing.

title: What UAE Finance Teams Actually Use ERP AI Assistants For
subtitle: Behind the marketing, the AI features getting daily use in Dubai and Abu Dhabi finance departments are narrow, repetitive and closely supervised.
excerpt: Bank reconciliation suggestions, invoice data capture and plain-language report queries are where AI assistants inside mid-market ERP are earning their keep, finance leaders say.
imageCaption: Dubai skyscrapers at dusk, with light trails on Sheikh Zayed Road.
keyTakeaways: The most-used AI features are matching suggestions in bank reconciliation and data capture from supplier invoices.
Finance teams keep a human approval step on anything that posts to the ledger.
Arabic-language supplier documents remain a weak spot for some extraction tools, so buyers should test with their own samples.
content: Almost every mid-market ERP and accounting platform sold in the UAE now advertises some form of AI assistant. To find out which features are actually used, we asked finance managers and controllers at a dozen Dubai and Abu Dhabi companies, ranging from trading houses to professional services firms, what they rely on week to week. The answers were consistent and more modest than vendor launch material might suggest.

The clear favourite is reconciliation support: the system proposes matches between bank statement lines and open invoices or bills, and an accountant accepts or rejects them. Close behind is data capture from supplier invoices, where a scanned or emailed PDF is turned into a draft bill with supplier, amounts and VAT pre-filled. Both tasks are repetitive, easy to check and quick to correct when the suggestion is wrong.

Natural-language reporting, where a manager types a question such as which customers are more than 60 days overdue, is used but less often. Controllers said they value it for quick answers in meetings but still build formal management reports the traditional way, because they need to know exactly which filters and periods sit behind each figure. Some also use it to draft commentary for management packs, which they then edit.

No one we spoke to allows an assistant to post journal entries without review. Several also flagged that extraction quality drops on Arabic-only or bilingual supplier invoices, and recommended that buyers test any tool with a batch of their own local documents before relying on it for month-end. In practice, the assistant prepares the work and a person remains accountable for every entry that reaches the ledger, which is also what external auditors expect to see.

title: Doha Retailers Test AI Forecasting Features in Their Commerce and ERP Software
subtitle: Mid-sized Qatari retailers are switching on the demand-forecasting modules in their existing platforms for a few product lines first, wary of over-trusting models trained on short sales histories.
excerpt: With the cooler months bringing a busier shopping calendar, some Doha retailers are piloting the AI forecasting features built into their commerce and ERP software to cut both stock-outs and excess inventory.
imageCaption: A monitor displaying web analytics charts, with a plant in the background.
keyTakeaways: Retailers are piloting AI forecasting on a limited set of product lines rather than across the whole catalogue.
Short or disrupted sales histories make seasonal events such as Ramadan and the winter peak harder to model.
Forecast output only helps if it flows into purchasing and replenishment workflows that buyers already use.
content: For many retailers in Qatar, the period from November through to the spring brings a fuller calendar of events, tourism and family shopping than the summer months. That seasonality is exactly what makes forecasting difficult, and it is why several mid-sized Doha retailers we spoke to are piloting the AI demand-forecasting features now offered inside commerce platforms and ERP systems, often as an add-on to software they already pay for, rather than relying solely on last year's spreadsheets.

The pilots are deliberately narrow. Merchandise managers described choosing two or three categories with reliable sales data, such as fragrances, home goods or children's clothing, and comparing the tool's weekly forecasts against what their buyers would have ordered anyway. The test is not whether the model is perfect but whether it reduces the number of lines that run out early or sit unsold at the end of the season.

One recurring challenge is history. Store openings, format changes and shifting dates for Ramadan and Eid mean that two or three years of data may not contain a clean pattern. Retailers said the more useful tools let them flag promotions, holidays and one-off events manually, rather than expecting the model to infer everything from raw sales. Buyers said they also look for tools that explain the drivers behind a forecast.

Integration is the other deciding factor. A forecast that lives in a separate dashboard tends to be ignored. Teams reported better results when suggested order quantities appeared directly in the purchasing screens of their ERP or commerce platform, where buyers could accept or adjust them as part of their usual routine. Retailers whose commerce and ERP systems were already connected found the pilots far easier to run than those still exporting data by hand.

title: Omani SMEs Turn to AI Document Capture for Bilingual Paperwork
subtitle: Small finance teams in Muscat and Sohar are using AI extraction to cut manual keying of supplier bills, receipts and delivery notes.
excerpt: For businesses that still receive much of their paperwork on paper or as scanned PDFs, AI document capture is proving to be one of the more practical uses of AI.
imageCaption: A hand holding a phone calculator over a stack of printed invoices.
keyTakeaways: AI capture tools reduce manual data entry but still need a review step for amounts and VAT.
Bilingual and handwritten documents are where accuracy varies most between tools.
SMEs get the most value when captured data flows straight into their accounting software as draft bills.
content: In many Omani small and medium-sized businesses, the accounts function is one or two people. Much of their week goes on typing supplier invoices, fuel receipts and delivery notes into accounting software, often from documents that arrive on paper, as phone photos or as scanned PDFs mixing Arabic and English. It is a narrow, unglamorous task, and it is where several Muscat-based accountants told us AI has made the most noticeable difference.

Modern document capture tools, either built into cloud accounting platforms or sold as add-ons, read a document and propose the supplier, date, line items, totals and VAT. The accountant checks the draft and approves it. Users said the time saving is real on clean, typed invoices from regular suppliers, where the tool learns the layout after a few examples. Gains are smaller for irregular suppliers.

Accuracy is less consistent on bilingual documents, faded thermal receipts and anything handwritten. Accountants described a pattern of trusting the tool for supplier names and dates while always checking totals and tax amounts by eye. With VAT in place in Oman since 2021, getting the tax line right matters for returns and audits. Some tools let users correct a field once and remember the fix for that supplier.

Advisers recommend testing any tool on a month's worth of real paperwork before committing, and checking where documents are stored once uploaded. For businesses that handle customer or employee records alongside supplier bills, Oman's personal data protection rules are another reason to ask vendors clear questions about hosting and retention. They also suggest asking how long uploaded documents are kept and whether they are used to improve the vendor's models.

title: Kuwaiti Buyers Ask SaaS Vendors Where Their Data Will Live
subtitle: Kuwaiti IT managers are sorting business applications by sensitivity and asking each SaaS vendor for a clear answer on hosting region before they sign.
excerpt: The question for many Kuwaiti companies is no longer whether to use SaaS, but which hosting region each application's data sits in and what that choice costs.
imageCaption: Looking up at glass office towers against the sky.
keyTakeaways: Kuwaiti firms are classifying workloads by sensitivity before deciding where each should be hosted.
Regulated sectors such as banking face stricter expectations than most private-sector SMEs.
Latency, support hours and exit terms matter as much as headline hosting location.
content: For Kuwaiti companies replacing back-office systems with SaaS, the hosting conversation has become more nuanced. IT managers we spoke to described a shift away from a blanket rule, either everything on premises or any SaaS product on its default global hosting, towards an application-by-application decision about where data should sit and why. The result is often a mixed estate, with different hosting choices for different applications.

The starting point is usually classification. Financial ledgers, payroll and customer records are treated as the most sensitive, while collaboration tools, marketing platforms and project software are often seen as lower risk. Companies in regulated sectors, particularly banking and insurance, follow the expectations of their regulators, which typically set a higher bar for outsourcing and data location than applies to a trading company or a clinic.

subheadings.title: In-country, regional or global
paragraphs: Buyers now generally sort SaaS offers into three tiers: products that can be hosted inside Kuwait, often through a local partner, products that offer a Gulf hosting region in a neighbouring country, and products that run only on the vendor's default global infrastructure. Each has trade-offs. In-country options can simplify conversations with auditors and regulators but may mean a narrower choice of software. A Gulf region usually gives good latency and a wider catalogue, while default global hosting tends to be the cheapest and fastest to deploy.

Several IT managers said they increasingly ask SaaS vendors a simple question early in a sales process: in which country will our production data and backups be stored, and can that be written into the contract. Vendors that cannot give a clear answer tend to fall off shortlists. Some now include the question in their initial request for information, so that vendors self-select before demos are booked.

subheadings.title: Practical checks beyond location
paragraphs: Location is only one factor. Buyers also pointed to support availability during Kuwaiti working hours, Arabic-language documentation, the ability to export data in usable formats at the end of a contract, and clear incident notification terms. For many mid-market firms, those details decide the purchase once the hosting question has been settled. Clear service-level commitments and a named regional account contact also feature on many checklists.

title: UAE Procurement Teams Rethink SaaS Renewals and Multi-Year Commitments
subtitle: With software spend now a visible line in most budgets, Dubai and Abu Dhabi buyers are treating renewals as negotiations rather than formalities.
excerpt: Unused seats, automatic price uplifts and bundled add-ons are prompting UAE companies to bring more discipline to SaaS renewals.
imageCaption: A monitor displaying web analytics charts, with a plant in the background.
keyTakeaways: Procurement teams are starting renewal reviews 90 to 120 days before contract end dates.
Seat utilisation data is the strongest lever in renewal talks.
Multi-year terms can lock in pricing but reduce flexibility if headcount or strategy changes.
content: A few years ago, many UAE companies bought SaaS tools department by department, often on a credit card, with renewals handled automatically. Procurement and finance leaders we spoke to say that has changed. Software subscriptions now add up to a significant share of operating costs, and renewals are being pulled into the same review process as any other major supplier contract.

The most common first step is a utilisation check. Finance teams export login and activity data from their main platforms and compare it with the number of licences paid for. Several described finding a meaningful share of seats unused, typically from leavers, project teams that had wound down or users who had moved to a different tool. Those numbers become the basis for reducing seat counts or moving light users to cheaper tiers.

Timing is the second lever. Buyers who begin reviews three to four months before the renewal date said they have more room to compare alternatives, consolidate overlapping tools and negotiate. Those who leave it to the final weeks often find themselves accepting the vendor's standard uplift. Some companies now keep a simple renewal calendar, owned by procurement, that lists every subscription, its business owner and the date by which a decision is needed.

Multi-year deals remain a judgement call. They can secure price stability, which some CFOs value in a growing business, but they reduce flexibility if headcount falls or the company changes direction. Procurement leads recommended negotiating the right to reduce seats at each anniversary, and making sure data export terms are clear before signing a longer commitment. Caps on renewal price increases are another common request.

title: Choosing SaaS in Bahrain: An SME Checklist for VAT, Bilingual Invoices and Hosting
subtitle: Bahraini small businesses have more cloud software choice than ever. A short list of local requirements separates the products that fit from those that do not.
excerpt: Before signing up for an accounting, CRM or HR platform, Bahraini SMEs should check a handful of local details that global product pages rarely mention.
imageCaption: Server racks with network cabling inside a data centre.
keyTakeaways: Accounting SaaS used in Bahrain needs to handle local VAT rates and produce figures that support the return.
Bilingual Arabic and English invoice templates are a practical requirement for many customers and suppliers.
Hosting location and data export terms should be confirmed in writing, not assumed from a vendor's regional sales presence.
content: Small and medium-sized businesses in Bahrain can now choose from a wide range of cloud accounting, CRM and HR products, many of them sold through regional partners or direct online sign-up. Accountants and IT advisers in Manama who help SMEs choose software told us the products themselves are rarely the problem. The issues tend to come from local details that a global product page does not cover, and which only surface after a business has migrated its data.

VAT is the first. Bahrain introduced VAT in 2019 and has since raised the standard rate, so accounting software needs to support the current rate, zero-rated and exempt supplies, and reports that map cleanly onto the return. Advisers recommend running a sample month through any shortlisted product and comparing the output with the figures the business would file. Credit notes deserve a test too.

The second is language. Many Bahraini customers, government counterparts and suppliers expect invoices and statements that show Arabic and English together. Some products support bilingual templates out of the box, others need custom layouts or add-ons, and right-to-left rendering of Arabic text in PDFs is worth checking carefully. Advisers also suggest checking that customer names and addresses can be stored in both languages, so documents do not have to be edited by hand before they are sent.

The third is data. Bahrain has hosted hyperscale cloud infrastructure for several years, but that does not mean a given SaaS product stores its data there. Buyers should ask where data is hosted, how it is protected under Bahrain's Personal Data Protection Law, and how they can export a complete copy if they later switch provider. Clear written answers to those questions are a good sign.

title: Why GCC Mid-Market Firms Are Consolidating Their SaaS Stacks
subtitle: After years of adding point tools, many Gulf companies are trying to do more with fewer platforms. The trade-offs are not always obvious.
excerpt: Integration headaches, duplicated customer data and rising subscription bills are pushing mid-sized Gulf businesses toward suites. Our analysis looks at when that makes sense.

author.name: Tariq Al-Mansoor
author.role: Head of Regional ERP & AI Research

imageCaption: Aerial daytime view of the Riyadh skyline and the Kingdom Centre tower under a blue sky.
keyTakeaways: Consolidation is driven more by integration and data quality problems than by licence cost alone.
Suites reduce the number of vendors but can be weaker than specialist tools in specific functions.
A phased approach, starting with finance and CRM, is the most common path we see.
content: Across the Gulf, mid-sized companies that grew quickly over the past decade often ended up with a patchwork of software: one tool for CRM, another for invoicing, a third for HR, separate project and helpdesk systems, and spreadsheets holding them together. In conversations with finance and IT leaders in Riyadh, Dubai, Doha and Kuwait City, a common theme has emerged this year: a desire to bring that patchwork down to a smaller number of platforms.

Cost is part of the story, but it is rarely the main driver. The bigger issue is data. When a customer's details exist in four systems, each slightly different, reporting becomes unreliable and compliance tasks such as responding to a data subject request become slow. E-invoicing requirements in Saudi Arabia, and those being introduced in the UAE, add another reason to keep sales and finance data tightly connected.

subheadings.title: Suites versus best-of-breed
paragraphs: Suites from vendors such as Zoho and Odoo, and work-management platforms that extend into CRM and service desks, offer a single data model and one bill. The trade-off is depth. A specialist helpdesk or marketing automation product may offer features a suite module lacks, and teams that rely on those features can resist the move. In our view, the right answer depends on where the business differentiates. A company whose customer service is central to its brand may keep a specialist support tool and consolidate elsewhere. A distributor whose main pain is order-to-cash may prioritise a single ERP and CRM.

subheadings.title: How companies are phasing the change
paragraphs: The most common sequence we see starts with finance and CRM, because that is where duplicate data causes the most visible problems. HR and project tools follow once the core is stable. Leaders who have been through the process stressed two points: clean the data before migrating it, and budget time for staff training in both Arabic and English, rather than assuming people will adapt on their own.

title: Doha SMEs Rethink Supplier Payments as Digital Payables Tools Mature
subtitle: Cheques and manual bank transfers still dominate many Qatari small businesses' payables. A growing number are testing software that links bills, approvals and payment runs.
excerpt: Accounts payable automation, once mainly a large-enterprise tool, is reaching smaller Qatari firms through cloud accounting platforms and bank integrations.
imageCaption: A person typing on a laptop at a café table beside a drink.
keyTakeaways: Many Qatari SMEs still pay suppliers through a mix of cheques and manually keyed bank transfers.
Payables tools link supplier bills, approval workflows and payment batches in one place.
Bank connectivity and approval controls are the features owners scrutinise most closely.
content: Ask the owner of a small Doha trading or contracting business how suppliers get paid and the answer often involves a chequebook, a banking portal and a spreadsheet of who is owed what. Finance staff we spoke to described the familiar problems: duplicate payments, missed early-payment discounts, and hours spent each month answering supplier calls about when money will arrive.

Digital payables tools aim to tie those steps together. Supplier bills are captured into the accounting system, routed to the right manager for approval, scheduled according to due dates and then grouped into a payment batch that can be uploaded to, or in some cases sent directly to, the company's bank. Several cloud accounting platforms used in Qatar now include basic versions of this workflow, with specialist tools available for higher volumes.

Owners told us their main concerns are control and connectivity. They want to be certain that no payment leaves without the right approval, and they want the tool to work with their own bank rather than requiring a new account. Bank file formats and connectivity options vary, so checking this early avoids disappointment later. Multi-level approvals for larger amounts are a common request.

For companies that adopt these tools, the benefits tend to show up first as better visibility: a clear list of upcoming payments, fewer surprises at month-end and an audit trail that makes the annual review with external accountants easier. Over time, some also use that record to discuss better terms with key suppliers, because they can show a consistent history of paying on schedule. Advisers suggest starting with a single bank account and a small group of regular suppliers.

title: Bahraini SMEs Add Online Payment Links to Their Invoicing Software
subtitle: Connecting a payment gateway to cloud invoicing lets customers pay by card from the invoice itself. Manama businesses say the gains are real but the setup details matter.
excerpt: Pay-now buttons on invoices are becoming a standard feature of accounting SaaS. For Bahraini small businesses, the questions are which gateways connect, what fees apply and how payments reconcile.
imageCaption: Hands using a smartphone in front of a laptop.
keyTakeaways: Many cloud invoicing and accounting platforms can add a pay-now link to invoices through a connected payment gateway.
Gateway availability for Bahraini merchants differs by platform, so buyers should check supported providers before choosing software.
Automatic matching of gateway payouts, fees and invoices is what saves time at month-end.
content: For many small businesses in Bahrain, getting paid still means sending a PDF invoice and waiting for a bank transfer or a cheque. A growing number of owners we spoke to in Manama are adding a different option: a pay-now link on the invoice itself, connected to a payment gateway, so customers can settle by card or another online method in a few clicks.

Most widely used cloud invoicing and accounting platforms support this in some form. The business connects a gateway account to its software, and each invoice sent by email or shared as a link carries a payment button. When the customer pays, the invoice is marked as paid automatically. Owners said the main benefit is speed, particularly with smaller, repeat customers who would otherwise let invoices slip.

The setup details matter, however. Not every gateway that serves Bahraini merchants integrates with every accounting product, and the list of supported providers for the Gulf can be shorter than for other regions. Businesses should check which gateways their preferred software supports before committing, and understand the gateway's own merchant onboarding, settlement times and fees. Some gateways also require separate approval for recurring billing.

Reconciliation is the final consideration. Gateways typically pay out in batches with fees deducted, so the amount arriving in the bank rarely matches a single invoice. Accountants recommend choosing a setup where payouts, fees and individual invoices are matched automatically in the accounting system, rather than reconciled by hand at month-end. That way, the accounts show both the gross sale and the fees as separate, traceable entries.

title: Saudi Finance Teams Move Employee Spending Onto Managed Cards
subtitle: Petty cash and expense-claim spreadsheets are giving way to card programmes linked directly to accounting software, particularly among fast-growing Riyadh companies.
excerpt: Spend management platforms are attracting Saudi CFOs who want real-time control of employee spending and cleaner VAT records.
imageCaption: A laptop on a desk showing a sales analytics dashboard.
keyTakeaways: Managed card programmes let finance teams set limits by employee, merchant type or project.
Receipt capture at the point of purchase improves VAT recovery and reduces month-end chasing.
Integration with the accounting system is the feature CFOs most often cite as decisive.
content: For many Saudi companies, employee spending has long been handled through a mix of petty cash, personal cards and expense claims submitted weeks after the fact. Finance leaders we spoke to in Riyadh described the result as predictable: lost receipts, delayed reimbursements, and VAT that could not be reclaimed because the supporting invoice never reached the accounts team. The process also gave managers little visibility.

A growing number of companies, particularly in technology, professional services and retail, are moving that spending onto managed card programmes. Employees receive physical or virtual cards with limits set by role, merchant category or project. Each transaction appears in a central dashboard in near real time, and employees are prompted to photograph the receipt immediately. Cards can be frozen instantly if lost.

CFOs said the control features matter, but integration is what decides the purchase. Transactions need to arrive in the accounting system already categorised, with the receipt attached and VAT split out, so that month-end close does not turn into a reconciliation exercise. Buyers recommended testing this sync with their own chart of accounts during any trial. Mapping card categories to accounts is an early setup task.

There are also practical questions to ask before signing up: which bank or licensed provider issues the cards, how disputes and fraud are handled, whether the platform supports Arabic-language receipts, and how employee data is processed under the Kingdom's Personal Data Protection Law. CFOs also recommended starting with a single department, such as sales or operations, and setting clear policies on what can be bought before rolling cards out across the company.

title: Kuwaiti SMEs Move to Cloud Accounting: Bank Feeds and Multi-Currency Come First
subtitle: As small Kuwaiti businesses leave desktop accounting behind, connectivity with local banks and handling of foreign-currency trade are the first questions they ask.
excerpt: Cloud accounting adoption among Kuwaiti SMEs is growing steadily, but the features that matter most locally are not always the ones vendors lead with.
imageCaption: A person typing on a laptop at a café table beside a drink.
keyTakeaways: Direct bank feeds from Kuwaiti banks are not available in every platform, so statement import is still common.
Multi-currency support is essential for importers paying suppliers in US dollars, euros and other currencies.
The Kuwaiti dinar's three-decimal format is a small but important detail to verify.
content: Kuwait's small and medium-sized businesses have historically relied on desktop accounting packages or outsourced bookkeeping. Accountants and advisers we spoke to in Kuwait City say that is changing, with more owners moving to cloud platforms that let them see their numbers on a phone and share access with their external accountant. Mobile apps for approving bills and checking cash balances are a frequent reason owners give for the move.

The first question most owners ask is about the bank. Automatic bank feeds, which pull transactions into the accounting system each day, save hours of manual work. Coverage for Kuwaiti banks varies by platform, and where a direct feed is not available, businesses fall back on importing statement files. Advisers recommend confirming exactly which method works with the company's own bank before committing.

The second is currency. Many Kuwaiti SMEs import goods and pay suppliers in US dollars, euros or other currencies while selling locally in dinars. A platform needs to handle foreign-currency invoices, record exchange gains and losses correctly and produce reports in dinars. The Kuwaiti dinar's use of three decimal places is a small but real detail: some software handles it natively, while other tools need configuration to avoid rounding issues.

Beyond those basics, owners look for Arabic-language invoice templates, simple inventory tracking and the ability to give their accountant controlled access. Kuwait has not introduced VAT, which simplifies setup compared with neighbouring markets, though businesses trading across the Gulf still need software that can handle VAT on regional sales. Advisers recommend a trial using a real month of transactions before deciding.

title: Saudi Payroll Teams and Mudad: The Questions to Ask HR Software Vendors
subtitle: Wage Protection System compliance runs through Mudad. Before switching payroll software, Saudi HR and finance teams should test how a vendor handles it in practice.
excerpt: Payroll errors in Saudi Arabia can affect a company's compliance standing, not just employee morale. We set out what buyers should check when evaluating HR and payroll platforms.
imageCaption: A hand holding a phone calculator over a stack of printed invoices.
keyTakeaways: Saudi employers submit wage data for the Wage Protection System through the Mudad platform.
Buyers should test how a payroll tool produces and reconciles Mudad submissions with actual bank payments.
GOSI contributions, end-of-service calculations and Hijri and Gregorian date handling are other common sticking points.
content: Saudi Arabia's Wage Protection System requires employers to show that salaries are paid in line with employment contracts. Wage data is submitted through Mudad, the platform used by private-sector employers for payroll and WPS compliance. For HR and finance teams, that means payroll software is not just a calculation engine: it has to produce data that matches what is reported and what the bank actually pays.

Payroll managers we spoke to described the most common problems when changing systems. Allowances coded differently from the employment contract, mismatches between employee identifiers in the HR system and official records, and late changes after the payroll run has been finalised all create discrepancies that take time to resolve. Each of these needs to be corrected and resubmitted, which takes time during a busy month-end.

subheadings.title: What to test during a trial
paragraphs: Buyers should ask vendors to demonstrate a full payroll cycle using realistic data: monthly run, Mudad submission or file preparation, bank payment file, and reconciliation between the three. It is worth asking how the system handles mid-month joiners and leavers, unpaid leave, and retroactive salary changes, since these are where errors tend to appear. Teams should also check how the platform calculates GOSI contributions and end-of-service benefits under the Saudi Labour Law, and whether it handles both Hijri and Gregorian dates in contracts and payslips.

subheadings.title: Global payroll platforms and local partners
paragraphs: Companies hiring a small number of staff in the Kingdom sometimes use global employment or payroll platforms. In those cases, it is important to understand who is the legal employer, who handles Mudad and GOSI obligations, and how local payroll is processed. Several HR leaders said they ask for a named local contact and a written description of the compliance process before signing.

title: UAE E-Invoicing Programme: What Finance Teams Should Prepare Now
subtitle: The UAE's national e-invoicing programme is moving from announcement to implementation. Finance teams that start on data quality and system readiness now will have an easier transition.
excerpt: The UAE is introducing structured e-invoicing in phases. While details and dates should be checked against the latest Ministry of Finance and Federal Tax Authority guidance, the groundwork is the same for most businesses.
imageCaption: Downtown Dubai and the Burj Khalifa at sunset, above a highway interchange.
keyTakeaways: The UAE programme uses a model in which invoices are exchanged in a structured format through accredited service providers.
Rollout is phased, so businesses should confirm which phase applies to them from official guidance.
Master data quality, especially customer and supplier tax registration details, is the most common source of preparation work.
content: The UAE has announced a national e-invoicing programme that will replace PDF and paper invoices between businesses with structured electronic invoices. The model differs from Saudi Arabia's Fatoora system in its mechanics: rather than every invoice being cleared directly by the tax authority, invoices are exchanged through accredited service providers using a common framework, with tax data reported to the authorities. The programme is being introduced in phases, starting with larger businesses.

Because timelines and technical specifications have been updated as the programme has progressed, finance teams should rely on the latest Ministry of Finance and Federal Tax Authority publications for dates and requirements that apply to them. What does not change is the preparation work, and finance leaders we spoke to in Dubai and Abu Dhabi said much of it has little to do with technology.

subheadings.title: Start with the data
paragraphs: Structured e-invoices depend on accurate master data. Customer and supplier records need correct legal names, tax registration numbers and addresses. Product and service codes must be consistent. Several controllers said their first audit uncovered duplicate customers, missing registration numbers and free-text invoice lines that would not translate cleanly into a structured format. Cleaning that data takes time and needs input from sales, procurement and finance, so it is a sensible place to begin regardless of which phase a business falls into.

subheadings.title: System and provider readiness
paragraphs: Businesses should ask their ERP or accounting vendor how it plans to support the UAE framework, including integration with accredited service providers and handling of credit notes, self-billing and cross-border invoices. Companies that also operate in Saudi Arabia will want to understand how one system can meet both countries' requirements without duplicate processes. Finally, finance teams should plan for testing. Running a pilot with a handful of customers and suppliers before the mandatory date, where possible, gives time to resolve rejected invoices and process gaps.

title: Omani Logistics Firms Switch to Cloud Warehouse and Delivery Apps
subtitle: Mid-sized freight, warehousing and trucking operators in Oman are replacing paper picking lists and delivery notes with SaaS tools linked to their invoicing.
excerpt: Cloud warehouse management, proof-of-delivery apps and integrated invoicing are the first SaaS products Omani logistics companies are adopting.
imageCaption: A monitor displaying web analytics charts, with a plant in the background.
keyTakeaways: Warehouse management and proof-of-delivery apps are typically the first systems logistics firms digitise.
Linking operational data to invoicing shortens the time between delivery and payment.
Connectivity in remote areas and driver adoption are practical hurdles that pilots should test.
content: Logistics is one of the sectors Oman is counting on to diversify its economy, and much of the work is done by mid-sized operators: freight forwarders, warehouse operators and trucking companies whose day-to-day processes are often still run on paper and spreadsheets. Operations managers we spoke to in Muscat and Sohar said that is changing, as subscription software designed for smaller operators has become easier to buy and set up without a large IT team.

They described a common starting point. A cloud warehouse management system replaces manual stock counts and handwritten picking lists with barcode scanning and real-time inventory. A proof-of-delivery app lets drivers capture signatures, photos and timestamps on a phone, removing the need to return paper delivery notes to the office. Both are typically priced per user or per site, which managers said made a small pilot easy to justify.

The financial benefit often comes from connecting those operational systems to invoicing. When a delivery is confirmed in the app, an invoice can be raised immediately rather than days later, which managers said shortens the time to payment and reduces disputes because the evidence is attached. It also gives customers a digital record they can check, which several managers said has reduced the number of disputed invoices.

There are practical hurdles. Mobile coverage on some inland and coastal routes can be patchy, so apps need to work offline and sync later. Driver adoption also matters: managers recommended involving drivers in pilots, providing Arabic and English interfaces, and keeping the number of steps per delivery as small as possible. Pilots on one route or one warehouse help surface these issues early.

title: Selling to Gulf Governments: How E-Procurement Portals Shape Vendor Onboarding
subtitle: Government purchasing across the GCC now runs largely through digital portals. For software vendors, registration and compliance paperwork has become part of the sales cycle.
excerpt: From Saudi Arabia's Etimad platform to the e-procurement systems used elsewhere in the Gulf, digital portals now set the rules for how B2B suppliers reach public-sector buyers.

author.name: Tariq Al-Mansoor
author.role: Head of Regional ERP & AI Research

imageCaption: Looking up at glass office towers against the sky.
keyTakeaways: Public-sector tenders across the GCC are increasingly published, submitted and evaluated through online portals.
Registration requirements typically include local commercial registration, tax documents and sector-specific certifications.
Local content and data-residency expectations can affect how software vendors structure their bids.
content: For software companies hoping to sell to government entities in the Gulf, the first step is no longer a meeting. It is registration on a procurement portal. Saudi Arabia's Etimad platform handles a large share of government tenders in the Kingdom, and other GCC states operate their own digital procurement systems at federal, emirate or ministry level. These portals publish tenders, receive bids and record evaluations, and they set the documentation a vendor must have in place before it can compete.

Vendors we spoke to described registration as more demanding than many expect. Typical requirements include a local commercial registration, tax registration certificates, and in some cases chamber of commerce membership or sector-specific approvals. Documents may need to be submitted in Arabic, and expiry dates have to be tracked carefully, because a lapsed certificate can disqualify an otherwise strong bid. Renewals add more work.

Beyond paperwork, government buyers increasingly look at local content and data residency. Saudi Arabia, for example, gives weight to local content in government procurement, and many public-sector entities across the region expect data to be hosted within the country. Software vendors may need to show how their solution meets those expectations, sometimes through local partners or in-country hosting. Requirements differ between countries.

For smaller SaaS companies, the advice from those who have been through the process is consistent: assign someone to own portal registrations and renewals, keep a ready library of Arabic and English company documents, and read each tender's technical and compliance requirements in full before investing time in a bid. Partnering with an established local reseller is another route several vendors described.

title: What Saudi Arabia's Regional Headquarters Rules Mean for SaaS Vendors
subtitle: The Regional Headquarters Programme has made a Riyadh presence a practical consideration for international software companies that want to sell to Saudi government entities.
excerpt: For SaaS vendors with ambitions in Saudi public-sector work, the Regional Headquarters Programme is a strategic decision, not just a legal formality.
imageCaption: Aerial daytime view of the Riyadh skyline and the Kingdom Centre tower under a blue sky.
keyTakeaways: Saudi Arabia's Regional Headquarters Programme links eligibility for many government contracts to having a regional HQ in the Kingdom.
Exceptions and thresholds exist, so vendors should take specific legal advice rather than assume they are in or out of scope.
Vendors focused on private-sector customers face different, often lighter, considerations.
content: Saudi Arabia's Regional Headquarters Programme, launched in 2021, encourages multinational companies to base their Middle East headquarters in Riyadh. Since the start of 2024, government entities have been generally restricted from contracting with foreign companies that do not have a regional headquarters in the Kingdom, subject to exceptions. For international software vendors, the programme has turned a long-standing debate about where to locate a regional office into a concrete commercial question.

We spoke to executives at several international and regional SaaS companies about how they are approaching the decision. Their answers depended largely on one factor: how much of their Saudi pipeline comes from government and government-linked entities. For those with a large public-sector pipeline, the question is how and when to establish a qualifying presence. For those selling mainly to private companies, it is one consideration among several.

subheadings.title: Who is most affected
paragraphs: Vendors whose growth plans rely on ministries, public agencies or large state-linked companies described the programme as central to their strategy. For them, a Riyadh regional headquarters is a prerequisite for competing on many tenders, and they are weighing the cost of meeting its requirements against the size of that market. By contrast, vendors that sell mainly to private-sector SMEs and mid-market companies said the rules affect them less directly. Many serve Saudi customers through local partners or a smaller in-country entity, and are focusing instead on ZATCA e-invoicing integration, Arabic-language support and data-residency questions.

subheadings.title: Questions to work through
paragraphs: The programme includes thresholds, exemptions and specific requirements on activities and staffing, and these have been clarified over time. Executives stressed the importance of specialist legal advice rather than relying on summaries. Practical questions include which entities in the group would hold contracts, how regional staff would be distributed, and how the move affects tax and data-hosting arrangements. Several also noted that the decision is not only about compliance. A Riyadh base can bring vendors closer to customers and partners in the region's largest economy, which some see as a reason to move regardless of the government-contracting rules.

title: With Corporate Tax in Place, UAE Finance Teams Revisit Their Accounting Software
subtitle: The 9% federal corporate tax has raised the bar for record-keeping. Many UAE businesses are finding that systems set up for VAT alone are no longer enough.
excerpt: Corporate tax has pushed UAE finance teams to look again at how their accounting systems handle adjustments, related-party transactions and audit trails.
imageCaption: A laptop on a desk showing a sales analytics dashboard.
keyTakeaways: UAE corporate tax at 9% applies to taxable income above a threshold for financial years starting on or after 1 June 2023.
Finance teams need clearer tagging of non-deductible expenses, related-party transactions and adjustments.
Businesses on basic bookkeeping setups are upgrading software or chart-of-accounts structures to support tax computations.
content: The UAE's federal corporate tax, levied at 9% on taxable income above a threshold, applies to financial years starting on or after 1 June 2023. As businesses move through their first and second tax cycles, finance leaders we spoke to in Dubai and Abu Dhabi said the experience has prompted a closer look at their accounting systems, many of which were configured mainly with VAT in mind.

The pressure points are fairly consistent. Corporate tax calculations start from accounting profit and then require adjustments, for example for non-deductible expenses, certain entertainment costs and transactions with related parties. When those items are scattered across general expense accounts, preparing the computation becomes a manual exercise. Several controllers described restructuring their chart of accounts so that tax-relevant items are captured separately from the start.

Related-party and connected-person transactions have drawn particular attention. Groups with several UAE entities, or with owners who also control other businesses, need to document those transactions and show that they are on arm's-length terms. Accounting software that supports clear intercompany tagging and consolidated reporting makes that easier. Transfer pricing documentation requirements also apply to some groups, depending on their size, and advisers said software that keeps intercompany balances reconciled month by month makes that work easier.

For smaller businesses, the shift has often meant moving from basic bookkeeping to a proper cloud accounting platform, or engaging an accountant who requires one. Advisers emphasised that software is only part of the answer: good documentation, timely bookkeeping and an understanding of which reliefs and thresholds apply are just as important, and should be confirmed with a qualified tax adviser.

title: Qatar's Data Privacy Law and SaaS Contracts: What Doha Buyers Now Ask For
subtitle: Qatari companies are paying closer attention to how their CRM, HR and helpdesk subscriptions handle personal data, and are writing those expectations into contracts.
excerpt: Qatar's Personal Data Privacy Protection Law has been on the books since 2016. As more customer and employee data moves into SaaS, Doha buyers are turning its principles into concrete contract terms.
imageCaption: Looking up at glass office towers against the sky.
keyTakeaways: Qatar's Personal Data Privacy Protection Law (Law No. 13 of 2016) applies to personal data held in SaaS applications as much as on company servers.
Buyers are asking SaaS vendors for data processing terms covering purpose, security, sub-processors and cross-border transfers.
Breach notification commitments and data return at contract end are the clauses most often negotiated.
content: Qatar was among the first GCC states to adopt a comprehensive data protection law: the Personal Data Privacy Protection Law, Law No. 13 of 2016. For years, many businesses treated it mainly as a matter for their own IT systems. That view is changing as more customer, employee and patient data moves into subscription software, and legal and procurement teams in Doha told us they now treat SaaS contracts as one of the main places where the law's requirements are put into practice.

The starting point is usually a data processing agreement. Buyers want the vendor to commit to processing personal data only for the purposes the customer sets, to apply appropriate security controls, and to list the sub-processors it relies on, with notice of any changes. Several said they now decline to use a vendor's standard terms without reviewing these points first.

Cross-border transfer is the second area. Many SaaS products available in Qatar store data outside the country by default. Buyers are asking where data and backups are held, whether a Gulf hosting region is available, and what safeguards apply when data leaves Qatar. For organisations in regulated sectors or working with government entities, those answers can decide the purchase. Some vendors offer one.

Finally, buyers are negotiating what happens when something goes wrong or the contract ends: how quickly the vendor will report a security incident affecting their data, and how a complete copy of the data will be returned and then deleted. Lawyers we spoke to recommended that companies check the law's current requirements and any guidance from the competent authority with specialist advisers, rather than relying on templates written for other jurisdictions.

title: Kuwaiti Family Businesses Modernise Back Offices as a New Generation Takes the Lead
subtitle: Succession is prompting many established Kuwaiti family groups to replace legacy systems and informal processes with modern ERP and reporting.
excerpt: In family-owned groups across Kuwait, a generational shift in leadership is often the moment when long-delayed technology decisions finally get made.
imageCaption: A laptop on a desk showing a sales analytics dashboard.
keyTakeaways: Leadership transitions are a common trigger for ERP and reporting projects in Kuwaiti family groups.
Group-level visibility across multiple companies is often the main goal.
Change management with long-serving staff is as important as software selection.
content: Family-owned groups remain central to Kuwait's private sector, spanning trading, retail, real estate, contracting and services. Many have grown over decades through a series of related companies, each with its own accounts, processes and often its own software. Advisers who work with these groups told us that a change in leadership, as a younger generation takes on executive roles, is frequently the moment when modernising the back office moves up the agenda.

The motivation is usually visibility. A new group chief executive or finance head often wants a consolidated view of performance across every company in the group, with consistent reporting and clear controls. When each entity uses a different accounting package, or relies heavily on spreadsheets and a few long-serving staff, producing that view is slow and difficult to verify. Lenders may ask for it too.

The projects we heard about typically start with a single ERP or accounting platform rolled out across group companies, standardised charts of accounts and a central reporting layer. Larger groups tend to consider established mid-market ERP products, while smaller ones often choose cloud suites that combine finance, CRM and HR. Implementation partners with experience in Kuwait are often chosen before the software itself, because local knowledge of reporting needs and staff expectations shapes the project.

Advisers stressed that the technology is rarely the hardest part. Long-serving managers may have built processes around personal knowledge, and moving to a shared system changes how decisions are made and who sees what. Projects that succeed tend to involve those managers early, train staff in Arabic and English, and phase the rollout company by company. The broader New Kuwait 2035 vision of a more diversified, private-sector-led economy gives these groups another reason to professionalise their operations.

title: Saudi PDPL in Practice: What Buyers Now Ask SaaS Vendors
subtitle: More than two years after enforcement began, Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law has changed the questions procurement and security teams put to software suppliers.
excerpt: Data location, breach notification and cross-border transfer safeguards now feature in most Saudi SaaS evaluations. We set out the questions buyers are asking.
imageCaption: Server racks with network cabling inside a data centre.
keyTakeaways: Saudi Arabia's PDPL has been enforced since September 2024, with SDAIA as the competent authority.
Buyers now routinely ask where data is stored, how cross-border transfers are justified and how quickly incidents are reported.
Vendors that provide clear written answers and contractual commitments move through procurement faster.
content: Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law came into force in 2023, with enforcement beginning in September 2024 after a transition period. The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, SDAIA, oversees it. Security and procurement leaders we spoke to in Riyadh said the law has steadily changed how they evaluate SaaS vendors, especially for platforms that hold customer, employee or patient data.

Where vendor security questionnaires once focused mainly on certifications and technical controls, they now include a substantial data protection section. Buyers want to understand not just whether data is secure, but where it is processed, by whom and on what legal basis. Many security teams have added a dedicated PDPL section to their standard questionnaire, and some ask vendors to complete it before a commercial proposal is considered.

subheadings.title: The questions buyers are asking
paragraphs: The most common questions concern location and transfer. Buyers ask where production data and backups are stored, whether any processing or support access happens outside the Kingdom, and what safeguards apply to such transfers under the PDPL and its regulations. They also ask which sub-processors the vendor uses and how they will be notified of changes. Incident response is the second focus. The implementing regulations set short deadlines for notifying the authority of qualifying personal data breaches, so buyers want vendors to commit to prompt notification so they can meet their own obligations. Contracts increasingly specify those timelines.

subheadings.title: Practical advice for both sides
paragraphs: For buyers, the advice from security leaders is to keep a record of processing activities that names each SaaS platform and the categories of data it holds, and to revisit vendor answers at renewal rather than only at onboarding. For vendors, the message is simple: prepare clear, written answers to these questions in Arabic and English, and be ready to reflect them in a data processing agreement. Several buyers said vendors that do this well move through procurement noticeably faster.

title: UAE Finance Teams Lean on Accounting Software Controls to Stop Invoice Fraud
subtitle: Fake bank-detail changes remain the cyber risk UAE finance teams meet most often. Approval workflows and audit logs already built into accounting and ERP SaaS are a large part of the defence.
excerpt: Finance leaders in Dubai and Abu Dhabi say attempts to redirect supplier payments are the incidents they see most. Many are responding by switching on controls their accounting software already offers.
imageCaption: Hands using a smartphone in front of a laptop.
keyTakeaways: Requests to change a supplier's bank details are the most common route for payment fraud.
Call-back verification using a known phone number is one of the most effective controls.
Accounting systems with approval workflows and change logs for supplier bank details help enforce good process.
content: When we asked finance leaders in Dubai and Abu Dhabi which cyber threats they encounter most often, the answer was rarely ransomware or advanced attacks. It was invoice fraud: emails, often from a genuine but compromised supplier account or a look-alike domain, asking for payment to a new bank account. The messages are usually well written, refer to real invoices and arrive at busy times such as month-end or before public holidays.

This kind of business email compromise relies on process gaps rather than technical vulnerabilities. If one person can change a supplier's bank details based on an email and then release payment, the organisation is exposed regardless of how strong its firewall is. Several CFOs told us their teams had intercepted attempts only because an experienced accountant noticed something unusual. Software can help close them.

The controls they now rely on are straightforward. Any request to change bank details is verified by calling the supplier on a number already held on file, never one provided in the email. Changes to supplier master data require approval by a second person, and the first payment to new details is flagged for extra review. Staff receive regular, short reminders with real examples.

Software helps enforce those rules. Accounting and ERP platforms that log every change to supplier bank details, require approval before changes take effect and separate the roles of preparing and releasing payments make it harder for a single mistake to cost the company money. Multi-factor authentication on email and finance systems remains the baseline. Several finance teams also restrict who can edit supplier records.

title: Bahraini SMEs Switch On the Security Settings Already in Their SaaS Apps
subtitle: Small businesses in Bahrain rarely have a security team, but the email, accounting and CRM subscriptions they rely on include controls that address many of the risks they face.
excerpt: Multi-factor authentication, user reviews and tested data exports are built into most business SaaS products. Manama IT advisers say too few SMEs turn them on.
imageCaption: A person typing on a laptop at a café table beside a drink.
keyTakeaways: Turning on multi-factor authentication for email, finance and CRM accounts is the single most valuable step for most SMEs.
Removing accounts for former staff and limiting admin rights reduce the impact of a compromise.
Backups only count if they have been restored successfully in a test.
content: Most small businesses in Bahrain run on a handful of cloud services: email, an accounting platform, perhaps a CRM and a file-sharing tool. Few have a dedicated security specialist. IT advisers in Manama who support SMEs told us that the incidents they see most often, such as compromised email accounts, unauthorised access by former staff and lost data, can largely be prevented with a short list of basic controls.

The first is multi-factor authentication. Most business SaaS platforms support it, often at no extra cost, but it is not always switched on by default. Advisers recommend enabling it for every user on email, finance and customer systems, starting with owners and anyone who can approve payments. Authenticator apps are generally preferred over SMS codes where available. It takes minutes per user.

The second is account hygiene. When an employee leaves, their access should be removed the same day, and shared logins should be replaced with individual accounts. Admin rights should be limited to the few people who need them. Advisers suggested a quarterly review of user lists in each system, which takes little time for a small company. Most SaaS admin panels make this easy.

The third is backups. Cloud platforms protect against hardware failure, but not always against accidental deletion or a compromised account. Businesses should know how their key data is backed up and, importantly, test restoring it. Combined with Bahrain's Personal Data Protection Law obligations to protect personal data, these steps give SMEs a realistic, affordable baseline. Many products offer a full export.

title: Oman's Data Protection Law: What Changes for CRM and Marketing Data
subtitle: With Oman's Personal Data Protection Law and its executive regulation in place, businesses are reviewing how they collect, store and use customer contact data.
excerpt: Marketing lists, CRM records and messaging campaigns all involve personal data. Omani businesses are reviewing consent, retention and vendor terms under the new framework.
imageCaption: Earth at night seen from orbit, with city lights visible.
keyTakeaways: Oman's Personal Data Protection Law, issued by Royal Decree 6/2022, is supported by an executive regulation.
Businesses are reviewing how consent is captured and recorded for marketing communications.
CRM and marketing platforms should support consent records, data subject requests and clear retention rules.
content: Oman's Personal Data Protection Law, issued by Royal Decree 6/2022, together with its executive regulation, sets rules for how organisations collect and process personal data. For many Omani businesses, the most immediate practical impact falls on the systems that hold the most customer data: CRM platforms, email marketing tools and messaging services. Those systems are often managed by marketing teams rather than IT, and may never have been reviewed.

Marketing and sales managers we spoke to in Muscat said their first task has been understanding what data they actually hold. Contact lists built up over years from events, website forms, purchased lists and business cards often lack any record of how each contact was obtained or whether they agreed to receive marketing. Several companies have chosen to clean or re-permission older lists rather than continue using them as they are.

Going forward, businesses are configuring their CRM and marketing platforms to capture consent at the point of collection and store it with the contact record. They are also setting retention periods, so inactive contacts are reviewed or removed, and documenting how they will respond if a customer asks to see, correct or delete their data. Most established platforms support these functions, but they need to be switched on and used consistently.

Vendor terms are the final piece. Businesses should understand where their CRM or marketing platform stores data, which sub-processors it uses and how it handles cross-border transfers. Because the law's requirements are detailed and specific to Oman, legal advisers recommend that companies seek specialist advice on their own circumstances rather than relying on general guides. Contracts should reflect the answers.

title: UAE Support Teams Work on Arabic Search Inside Their Helpdesk Knowledge Bases
subtitle: Customers who search a help centre in Arabic often get poor results, and Dubai support managers are finding the fix is as much about content as about the search engine.
excerpt: AI-assisted search is now standard in helpdesk software, but UAE support teams say Arabic queries only return useful answers when articles are written and tagged with Arabic searchers in mind.
imageCaption: A green paper speech bubble beside crumpled yellow paper on a yellow background.
keyTakeaways: Arabic help-centre searches often fail because articles exist only in English or use formal wording customers do not type.
AI answer features inside helpdesk platforms depend on the quality of the underlying Arabic articles.
Support teams are reviewing failed-search reports to decide which Arabic articles to write next.
content: Most helpdesk platforms sold in the UAE now include a self-service help centre with AI-assisted search, and many can generate a suggested answer from existing articles. Support managers at Dubai retailers, property firms and service companies told us the feature works well in English. In Arabic, results have been patchier, and the reasons are more often found in the knowledge base itself than in the software.

The most common problem is simple: the article a customer needs exists only in English. Where Arabic versions do exist, they are often formal translations, while customers type short, colloquial queries, sometimes in Arabic written with Latin letters. Spelling variations, missing diacritics and different words for the same product all reduce the chance of a match. A search that returns nothing pushes the customer straight back to a live agent.

Teams that have improved results describe a similar process. They export the list of searches that returned no useful result, group them by topic, and write or rewrite Arabic articles to match the words customers actually use. Some add common alternative spellings as tags or keywords. They also review AI-generated answers in Arabic before turning them on for customers, because a confident but wrong answer is worse than none.

Managers recommend that buyers comparing helpdesk tools test search with a real set of Arabic queries taken from their own chat and email history, rather than relying on a demo. They also suggest checking whether the platform reports failed searches by language, since that report becomes the team's to-do list once the help centre is live.

title: Saudi Online Retailers Prepare CRM Chatbots for the November Sales Peak
subtitle: Ahead of the busiest weeks of the year, e-commerce teams in Riyadh and Jeddah are tightening the scripts, hand-off rules and Arabic replies in the chatbots built into their CRM and messaging tools.
excerpt: Order-status questions can multiply during sale periods. Saudi retailers are using the bot features already inside their CRM platforms to absorb the routine queries, while keeping a clear route to a human agent.

author.name: Tariq Al-Mansoor
author.role: Head of Regional ERP & AI Research

imageCaption: Hands using a smartphone in front of a laptop.
keyTakeaways: Retailers are limiting bots to a short list of high-volume questions such as order status, delivery times and returns.
A fast, visible hand-off to a human agent matters more to customers than a clever bot.
Bots that read order data from the CRM or commerce platform need careful permission settings and testing before the peak.
content: For Saudi online retailers, the weeks around the November sales season bring a sharp rise in customer messages, most of them asking the same few questions. Where is my order, when will it arrive, and how do I return it. E-commerce managers we spoke to in Riyadh and Jeddah said they are preparing by tightening the chatbot features built into their CRM and messaging platforms rather than adding new tools at short notice.

The emphasis this year is on narrow scope. Rather than letting a bot attempt any question, teams are restricting it to a handful of intents where it can pull a definite answer from order or shipping data. Anything outside that list, or any message that expresses frustration, is passed to a person. Several managers said earlier, broader bots had generated complaints because customers felt stuck in loops.

subheadings.title: Getting the Arabic right
paragraphs: Retailers said the quality of Arabic replies is the area most likely to need work. Bots configured from English templates can produce stiff or overly formal responses, and customers mix Saudi dialect, Modern Standard Arabic and English in the same chat. Teams are rewriting the main replies in natural, polite Saudi Arabic, checking how the bot handles Arabic and Latin numerals in order numbers, and testing with staff who were not involved in building the flows.

subheadings.title: Testing before the rush
paragraphs: Because order-status bots read live data, managers are reviewing exactly what the bot can see and share. A bot should confirm the customer's identity before revealing delivery addresses or order contents, in line with the Kingdom's Personal Data Protection Law. Retailers are also running load tests with their vendors, agreeing escalation contacts for the peak weeks, and preparing a fallback message in case an integration fails on the busiest day.

title: Kuwaiti HR Teams Test Arabic CV Parsing in Their Recruitment Software
subtitle: Applicant tracking systems promise to read CVs automatically, but Kuwaiti recruiters say Arabic and bilingual CVs are where the parsing and AI ranking features need the closest checking.
excerpt: Kuwaiti employers moving hiring onto cloud recruitment platforms are finding that automated CV reading works well in English and less reliably on Arabic documents, and are adjusting their processes accordingly.
imageCaption: A person typing on a laptop at a café table beside a drink.
keyTakeaways: CV parsing in many applicant tracking systems is more accurate on English documents than on Arabic or bilingual ones.
Recruiters are keeping a human review of every shortlist rather than relying on automated ranking.
Candidate data held in recruitment software should have clear retention rules and access controls.
content: Recruitment has been one of the later HR processes to move onto cloud software in many Kuwaiti companies, but applicant tracking systems are now common among larger employers and growing among mid-sized firms. HR managers we spoke to said the main attractions are a single inbox for applications, structured interview feedback and automatic reading of CVs into candidate profiles. It is that last feature that has drawn the most comment.

When a CV is uploaded, the system extracts names, contact details, employers, dates and qualifications. Recruiters said this works well on English CVs with standard layouts. Arabic CVs, bilingual documents, and designs with columns or tables produce more errors, such as names split incorrectly, dates misread or Arabic job titles left blank. Several teams now spot-check every parsed profile from Arabic applications before it moves forward.

AI ranking, where the system scores candidates against a job description, is treated with more caution still. Recruiters worry that a candidate whose experience is described in Arabic, or with job titles common in Kuwait but not in the model's training data, may be ranked lower without good reason. Most of those we spoke to use scores as a sorting aid only, and read every application for shortlisted roles themselves.

HR leaders also flagged data handling. Recruitment systems collect personal information from people who never become employees, so employers are setting retention periods for unsuccessful applications and limiting who can view them. Buyers comparing platforms should test parsing with a sample of their own past CVs, with consent or anonymised, before relying on it in live hiring.

title: Doha Managers Ask for Arabic Dashboards and Plain-Language Queries in BI Tools
subtitle: Qatari companies rolling out business intelligence software beyond the finance team are asking whether dashboards render properly in Arabic and whether managers can ask questions in their own words.
excerpt: As reporting tools spread from analysts to line managers in Qatar, right-to-left layouts, Arabic labels and natural-language questions are moving up buyers' lists.
imageCaption: A monitor displaying web analytics charts, with a plant in the background.
keyTakeaways: Arabic support in BI tools varies from full right-to-left layouts to translated menus only.
Natural-language query features are useful for quick questions but depend on well-named, well-defined data.
Agreeing a single definition for each key figure matters more than the choice of tool.
content: Business intelligence software used to sit mainly with analysts and the finance team in Qatari companies. Managers we spoke to in Doha said that is changing, as sales heads, branch managers and operations leads are given their own dashboards inside reporting tools or the analytics modules of their ERP and CRM platforms. Wider use has brought new requirements, and Arabic support is near the top of the list.

Arabic support turns out to mean several different things. Some tools offer full right-to-left dashboards, with charts, tables and axis labels mirrored and Arabic fonts that render cleanly. Others translate menus but leave charts left-to-right, or struggle with mixed Arabic and English labels. Buyers said the only reliable way to judge is to build a real dashboard, with their own Arabic product and branch names, during the trial.

Natural-language querying, where a manager types a question and the tool builds a chart, is the AI feature attracting most interest. Users said it works well for simple questions once the underlying data is clearly named and structured. It is less reliable when terms are ambiguous, for instance when sales could mean orders, invoices or cash received. Questions typed in Arabic are supported by some tools and not others.

Analytics leads advised that companies agree definitions for their main figures before opening up dashboards and AI queries to a wider group. Without that, different managers can get different answers to what sounds like the same question, and confidence in the whole system drops. Access controls also need attention, so that branch managers see their own figures and not the whole company's.

title: Saudi Merchants Build Arabic-First Storefronts on E-Commerce Platforms
subtitle: Saudi brands selling online are treating Arabic as the default storefront language and checking how their e-commerce platform handles right-to-left themes, local payment methods and compliant invoices.
excerpt: Choosing an e-commerce platform in Saudi Arabia now starts with how well it supports an Arabic storefront, followed closely by payments, delivery integrations and e-invoicing.
imageCaption: A laptop showing a sales analytics dashboard on a desk.
keyTakeaways: Saudi merchants increasingly design the Arabic storefront first and treat English as the secondary language.
Right-to-left theme quality, Arabic search and local payment options are the most tested features.
