Invoices issued from the store must fit the merchant's ZATCA e-invoicing obligations.
content: For many Saudi brands launching or rebuilding an online store, the order of priorities has flipped. A few years ago, merchants often built an English site and added Arabic later. Founders and e-commerce managers we spoke to in Riyadh and Jeddah now start with Arabic, designing navigation, product names and checkout copy for Arabic-speaking shoppers first, then adapting for English.

That choice shapes which e-commerce platform they pick. Merchants told us the gap between platforms is widest not in core features, which are broadly similar, but in how well themes handle right-to-left layouts, how Arabic product search behaves, and whether apps and plug-ins added later respect the Arabic layout or break it. Several said they had moved platforms once already because a theme or checkout looked broken in Arabic on mobile.

subheadings.title: What merchants test
paragraphs: The merchants we spoke to described testing a short list of practical points during trials. Does the checkout display correctly in Arabic on a small phone screen. Do product filters work with Arabic attribute names. Are order confirmation emails and SMS messages available in Arabic. Are popular local payment methods and buy-now-pay-later options offered at checkout, and do the delivery integrations cover the couriers they actually use across the Kingdom's main cities and beyond. Several also stressed testing search with the misspellings and dialect words customers really type, since shoppers who cannot find a product rarely try a second time.

subheadings.title: Invoices and tax
paragraphs: Every sale generates an invoice, and Saudi merchants must issue those invoices in line with ZATCA's e-invoicing requirements, which have been rolled out to businesses in integration waves. Some e-commerce platforms handle this through apps or a connected accounting or ERP system rather than natively. Merchants are advised to confirm exactly how compliant invoices will be produced, and to check ZATCA's latest guidance for their own wave.

title: How UAE Free-Zone Companies Choose Their First SaaS Stack
subtitle: Newly licensed free-zone businesses in Dubai and Abu Dhabi are picking accounting, CRM and HR software in their first months, and the decisions they make early tend to stick.
excerpt: For a new free-zone company, the first software choices are usually made in a hurry. Advisers say a few questions about tax, invoicing and growth can save a painful migration later.
imageCaption: Dubai skyscrapers at dusk, with light trails on Sheikh Zayed Road.
keyTakeaways: Accounting software is usually the first purchase, driven by VAT and corporate tax record-keeping.
Free-zone businesses still need records that support corporate tax filings, even where a 0% rate may apply to qualifying income.
Choosing tools that export data cleanly makes a later move to a larger system easier.
content: Thousands of new companies are licensed in UAE free zones each year, and most need business software almost immediately. Founders and the accountants who support them told us the first purchase is nearly always cloud accounting, followed by a CRM and, once the team grows past a handful of people, an HR and payroll tool. Those early choices are often made quickly and then stay in place for years.

Tax is the main driver for accounting software. Free-zone companies are within the scope of UAE corporate tax, which applies at 9% for financial years starting on or after 1 June 2023, and must register even where they expect to qualify for a 0% rate on qualifying income. Meeting the conditions depends on keeping clean, well-separated records, so accountants push founders towards software that tracks income types clearly.

For CRM, founders tend to start with whatever their sales lead has used before. Advisers suggest checking whether the CRM connects to the accounting tool for quotes and invoices, whether it supports WhatsApp messaging, and how pricing changes as the team grows. HR tools are chosen later, usually when the company needs to track leave, visas and end-of-service entitlements in one place.

The most common piece of advice was to think about exit from the start. Founders who choose tools with clean data export and widely used integrations find it easier to move to a larger ERP or a different CRM later. Advisers also recommend checking each tool's support for the UAE's e-invoicing programme as it rolls out, and following the Federal Tax Authority's latest guidance.

title: Bahrain's SaaS Resellers Shift From Selling Licences to Running Implementations
subtitle: Local partners in Manama say their value to clients now lies in setup, data migration, Arabic configuration and ongoing support rather than in the subscription itself.
excerpt: As more SaaS vendors sell directly online, Bahraini resellers are repositioning as implementation and support partners for SMEs that lack in-house IT teams.
imageCaption: Looking up at glass office towers against the sky.
keyTakeaways: Bahraini resellers are earning more from setup, migration and support than from licence margins.
SMEs value local partners for Arabic configuration, VAT setup and on-site training.
Buyers should agree the scope, support hours and data ownership in writing before a project starts.
content: For years, much of Bahrain's business software market ran through local resellers who sold licences and installed systems on site. With most products now sold as subscriptions, often bought directly from a vendor's website, that model has changed. Partners we spoke to in Manama said licence margins have narrowed, and their business now depends on the services wrapped around the software.

Those services cover the work many SMEs cannot do alone: configuring the chart of accounts and VAT settings, migrating customer and stock data from spreadsheets or older systems, setting up Arabic invoice templates, building reports and training staff. Several partners said clients increasingly ask for a fixed-price package covering setup and the first months of support, rather than open-ended consultancy billed by the hour.

Business owners described a mixed picture. A good local partner shortens the path to a working system and is available in the same time zone and language. A weak one can leave a company with a half-configured system and little documentation. Owners who were happy with their partner said the key was clear scope at the start and a named contact who stayed with the project.

Advisers recommend that SMEs confirm in writing who holds the administrator access to their subscription, so that the business, not the partner, owns its data and account. They also suggest asking for references from similar-sized clients and checking whether the partner is formally recognised by the vendor, which can matter when an issue needs to be escalated.

title: Omani Hotels and Tour Operators Update Booking Software Before the Winter Season
subtitle: Smaller hotels, guesthouses and activity operators are moving reservations, channel management and payments onto cloud platforms ahead of Oman's busiest tourism months.
excerpt: With the cooler months approaching, independent hospitality businesses across Oman are replacing spreadsheets and phone bookings with cloud reservation tools that connect to online travel sites.
imageCaption: A person typing on a laptop at a café table beside a drink.
keyTakeaways: Channel managers that sync availability across booking sites are the most sought-after feature for small hotels.
Online deposits and payment links are reducing no-shows for activity and tour operators.
Owners should check VAT handling on invoices and how guest data is stored.
content: Oman's tourism calendar peaks in the cooler months, and for independent hotels, desert camps, guesthouses and tour operators, the autumn is when systems need to be ready. Owners and managers we spoke to in Muscat, Nizwa and Salalah said this year more of them have moved reservations onto cloud booking platforms, replacing a mix of spreadsheets, phone calls and messages that became hard to manage when demand rose.

For small hotels, the most valued feature is the channel manager, which keeps room availability synchronised across the property's own website and the online travel agencies it sells through. Managers said double bookings had been their biggest source of complaints in past seasons. A cloud property management system with a channel manager attached lets a small front-desk team see every booking in one place.

Tour and activity operators have different priorities. They want online booking pages in Arabic and English, deposits taken at the time of booking, and automatic reminders sent by message or email. Several said taking a deposit through a payment link had cut no-shows noticeably, though they also had to think carefully about refund rules for weather-related cancellations.

Advisers suggested a few checks before committing. Invoices should show VAT correctly, since Oman has applied VAT since 2021. Owners should confirm where guest passport and contact details are stored and who can access them, given Oman's personal data protection rules. And they should test the system on a phone, because many bookings and check-ins are now handled away from a desk.

title: Kuwaiti Restaurants Connect Their POS Systems to Cloud Accounting
subtitle: Cafés and restaurant groups in Kuwait are linking point-of-sale data directly to their accounting software to speed up daily reconciliation across branches.
excerpt: Manual end-of-day reports are giving way to automatic sales summaries flowing from POS terminals into cloud accounting, though owners say the mapping needs care at the start.
imageCaption: A hand holding a phone calculator over printed invoices.
keyTakeaways: Daily sales summaries posted automatically from POS to accounting reduce manual entry and errors.
Correctly mapping payment types, delivery-app sales and discounts is the hardest part of setup.
Card and delivery-platform settlements still need to be reconciled against bank deposits.
content: Kuwait's food and beverage sector is busy and competitive, with many operators running several branches and selling through dine-in, takeaway and delivery apps at the same time. Owners and finance managers we spoke to said the daily task of turning till reports into accounting entries had become one of the most time-consuming parts of the back office, especially for groups with more than two or three outlets.

The change they describe is a direct integration between the point-of-sale system and cloud accounting software. At the end of each day, the POS sends a summary of sales by category, payment method and branch, which arrives as a draft entry for the accountant to review. Most modern cloud POS products offer this, either built in or through a connector.

Setup is where the effort lies. Each payment type, whether cash, card, a delivery platform or a voucher, must be mapped to the right account, as must discounts, refunds and staff meals. Owners said getting this wrong at the start created weeks of corrections. Several recommended running the integration in parallel with the old process for a month before switching fully.

The integration does not remove reconciliation. Card settlements and delivery-platform payouts arrive in the bank days later and net of fees, so they still need to be matched against the recorded sales. Finance managers said that step became far quicker once sales data was flowing automatically, and that the bigger benefit was seeing branch performance daily rather than at month end.

title: Saudi SaaS Startups Rework Subscription Billing for SAR Pricing and E-Invoicing
subtitle: Founders selling software subscriptions to Saudi businesses are moving away from US-dollar price lists and checking that their billing tools can issue compliant invoices.
excerpt: Local software startups say pricing in riyals, offering annual invoicing and fitting subscription billing into ZATCA's e-invoicing rules are now basic requirements for winning Saudi business customers.

author.name: Tariq Al-Mansoor
author.role: Head of Regional ERP & AI Research

imageCaption: An aerial daytime view of the Riyadh skyline with the Kingdom Centre tower under a blue sky.
keyTakeaways: Saudi business buyers increasingly expect SaaS prices quoted and invoiced in riyals.
Many customers prefer annual invoices paid by bank transfer rather than monthly card charges.
Subscription billing tools need to produce invoices that meet ZATCA e-invoicing requirements for the seller's situation.
content: Saudi Arabia's software startup scene has grown quickly, and many young companies now sell subscriptions to other Saudi businesses. Founders we spoke to in Riyadh said that, after building the product, billing turned out to be one of the more complicated parts of the business. Tools designed for global SaaS companies do not always match how Saudi customers buy, pay or need to be invoiced.

The first change most made was currency. Startups that began with US-dollar pricing found procurement teams preferred quotes in riyals, which avoided internal questions about exchange rates and matched budget lines. Founders said switching to SAR price lists, with VAT shown clearly, shortened approval times. Some keep dollar prices only for customers outside the Kingdom.

subheadings.title: How customers want to pay
paragraphs: Payment habits are the second adjustment. Smaller customers are comfortable with monthly card payments, but larger companies and government-linked entities often require an invoice, a purchase order reference and payment by bank transfer, usually annually or quarterly. Founders said their billing system needs to handle both, along with credit notes, mid-term upgrades and proration, without the finance team rebuilding invoices by hand.

subheadings.title: Fitting into e-invoicing
paragraphs: Every invoice a Saudi VAT-registered startup issues must follow ZATCA's e-invoicing rules, and businesses are brought into the integration phase in waves. A subscription billing tool that generates invoices outside the company's compliant system can create gaps. Founders are either choosing billing tools that connect to a compliant accounting or ERP system or issuing invoices from that system directly, and are advised to check ZATCA's latest guidance for their own obligations.

title: UAE Contractors Move Progress Billing and Retentions Into Project Software
subtitle: Mid-sized contractors and fit-out firms in Dubai and Abu Dhabi are replacing spreadsheet payment applications with construction and ERP software that tracks claims, variations and retentions.
excerpt: Payment applications, variation orders and retention balances have long lived in spreadsheets at many UAE contractors. More firms are now moving them into connected project and finance software.

author.name: Tariq Al-Mansoor
author.role: Head of Regional ERP & AI Research

imageCaption: Dubai skyscrapers at dusk, with light trails on Sheikh Zayed Road.
keyTakeaways: Contractors want payment applications, variations and retentions tracked against the same contract record.
Linking project progress to invoicing reduces disputes over what has been claimed and certified.
VAT treatment of progress payments and retentions should be confirmed with advisers and set up correctly in the software.
content: Construction and fit-out firms in the UAE run on cash flow, and cash flow depends on getting monthly payment applications right. Commercial managers at mid-sized contractors told us that, for many firms, the claim process still relies on spreadsheets passed between site teams, quantity surveyors and finance. Each version is slightly different, and tracking what has been claimed, certified and paid across dozens of projects is hard.

Firms making the change are moving this work into construction management software or the project modules of their ERP. Each contract is set up with its schedule of values, and every month the team records progress against each line. The system calculates the claim, deducts retention and previous payments, adds approved variations, and produces the application and, once certified, the invoice.

Commercial managers said the biggest benefit is a single record. When a client queries a claim, the team can show the history of every line, variation and certification without searching through email. Subcontractor payments can be handled in the same way, so the firm can see what it owes down the chain alongside what it is owed.

Finance teams highlighted tax as an area for care. The VAT treatment of progress payments and retentions has specific rules, and corporate tax adds further record-keeping expectations. Firms are advised to agree the correct treatment with their tax advisers and then configure the software to match, rather than relying on default settings, and to check the Federal Tax Authority's latest guidance.

title: Bahraini Accountants Lean on VAT Reports Built Into Cloud Accounting Software
subtitle: Small practices and in-house accountants in Bahrain say well-configured tax codes and built-in VAT reports have cut the time spent preparing returns, but setup mistakes still cause trouble.
excerpt: Most cloud accounting platforms sold in Bahrain can now produce a VAT summary ready for filing. Accountants say the report is only as good as the tax codes behind it.
imageCaption: A hand holding a phone calculator over printed invoices.
keyTakeaways: Built-in VAT reports save time only when every transaction carries the correct tax code.
Zero-rated, exempt and out-of-scope items are where setup errors most often appear.
Accountants recommend a monthly review of tax codes rather than a scramble before each filing.
content: Bahrain introduced VAT in 2019, and the standard rate has been 10 per cent since 2022. For small businesses, the quarterly or monthly return is one of the most regular compliance tasks, and accountants in Manama told us that cloud accounting software has changed how it is prepared. Most platforms sold in the Kingdom can produce a VAT summary that maps directly to the figures needed for filing.

That convenience depends entirely on tax codes. Every sale and purchase must carry the right code, whether standard-rated, zero-rated, exempt or out of scope. Accountants said the most common errors come from items set up once with the wrong default, such as an exempt service coded as standard-rated, or imported services that need reverse-charge treatment but are entered as ordinary purchases.

Practices that handle many small clients described a routine of reviewing tax codes monthly rather than waiting for the return deadline. They run an exception report listing unusual codes or missing tax, fix problems while the transactions are fresh, and keep notes explaining any judgement calls. Several said this has made returns quicker and given them more confidence if the National Bureau for Revenue asks questions.

For businesses choosing software, accountants suggested checking that the VAT report matches the structure of the Bahraini return, that bilingual tax invoices can be produced, and that records can be kept and retrieved for the required period. They also advised following the National Bureau for Revenue's latest guidance, as reporting requirements and any future e-invoicing plans may change.

title: Qatari Facilities Firms Move Maintenance Teams Onto Field-Service Apps
subtitle: Facilities management companies in Doha are replacing paper job cards and phone dispatch with cloud field-service software that technicians use on their phones.
excerpt: Work orders, technician scheduling and proof of completion are moving onto mobile apps at Qatari facilities firms, driven by client demands for faster response and clearer reporting.
imageCaption: Looking up at glass office towers against the sky.
keyTakeaways: Clients increasingly expect facilities contractors to report response times and completion evidence digitally.
Technician apps need to work in several languages and cope with weak signal in plant rooms and basements.
Linking completed work orders to invoicing and parts usage is where firms see the financial benefit.
content: Facilities management is a large and labour-intensive business in Qatar, covering towers, residential compounds, retail centres and public buildings. Operations managers at Doha facilities firms told us their clients now expect more than a monthly summary report. They want to see when a fault was logged, when a technician arrived, what was done and photographic proof, often through a portal they can check themselves.

That expectation has pushed firms towards cloud field-service software. A fault reported by a tenant or building manager becomes a work order, which a dispatcher assigns to a technician based on skills, location and availability. The technician receives it on a phone, records time on site, adds photos and parts used, and captures a sign-off. Planned preventive maintenance is scheduled in the same system.

subheadings.title: Designing for the technicians
paragraphs: Managers said adoption depends on the people using the app every day. Technicians come from many countries, so the app needs to work in several languages, with clear icons and minimal typing. Plant rooms and basements often have poor mobile signal, so offline mode, where the app saves work and syncs later, was cited as essential. Firms that involved senior technicians in testing reported fewer complaints after launch.

subheadings.title: Connecting to the back office
paragraphs: The financial benefit comes when field data flows into the rest of the business. Completed work orders can trigger invoices for chargeable jobs, parts used can update stock levels, and technician hours can feed into payroll and contract profitability reports. Firms that kept field service separate from their ERP or accounting system said they captured the operational gains but still spent days reconciling data at month end.

title: Omani Private Clinics Adopt Cloud Clinic Management and Online Booking
subtitle: Small private clinics in Muscat and beyond are moving appointments, reminders and billing onto cloud clinic-management software, with careful attention to how patient data is handled.
excerpt: Online booking and automatic reminders are the features drawing independent clinics in Oman to cloud practice software, while data protection shapes how they configure it.
imageCaption: Hands using a smartphone in front of a laptop.
keyTakeaways: Online booking and message reminders are the most valued features for small clinics.
Clinics are separating administrative data from clinical records and limiting who can see each.
Health information is treated as sensitive under data protection rules, so hosting and access terms need close review.
content: Independent dental, dermatology, physiotherapy and family clinics make up a large part of Oman's private healthcare sector. Clinic managers we spoke to in Muscat and Sohar said that many still ran appointments from a desk diary or a basic local program until recently. The move to cloud clinic-management software has been driven mainly by patients, who increasingly expect to book online and receive reminders on their phones.

The features clinics use most are straightforward. An online booking page shows available slots by doctor and service, in Arabic and English. Patients receive confirmation and reminder messages, and can cancel or reschedule without calling. Managers said reminders alone had reduced missed appointments noticeably, which matters for small practices where an empty slot is lost income.

Billing is the second area, and for many owners the more important one. Clinic software produces invoices with VAT where applicable, records payments by card or cash, and in some cases prepares claims for insurers. Clinic owners said having appointments and billing in one system made daily reconciliation simpler and gave them a clearer view of which services and doctors were busiest.

Patient data is the area that needs most care. Health information receives extra protection under Oman's data protection law, and clinics must also follow health-sector rules. Advisers recommend that clinics confirm where the software stores data, restrict access to clinical notes to treating staff, keep an audit trail of who views records, and check the latest guidance from the relevant Omani authorities before going live.

title: Saudi Private Schools Move Admissions, Fees and Parent Messaging Onto One Platform
subtitle: Private and international schools in the Kingdom are consolidating admissions, fee collection and parent communication into cloud school-management software.
excerpt: School administrators in Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province say parent apps and online fee payment have become expected, and are choosing platforms that bring them together with student records.
imageCaption: An aerial daytime view of the Riyadh skyline with the Kingdom Centre tower under a blue sky.
keyTakeaways: Schools are replacing separate tools for admissions, fees and messaging with a single platform.
Bilingual parent apps and online fee payment with instalment plans are the most requested features.
Student data, including information about children, requires careful handling under the Personal Data Protection Law.
content: Private and international schools in Saudi Arabia have grown in number over recent years, and administrators we spoke to said their back offices have struggled to keep up. A typical school might use one tool for online admissions, a spreadsheet for fees, a messaging app for parent communication and a separate system for grades and attendance. Each holds part of the picture, and staff spend time copying data between them.

The move now is towards cloud school-management platforms that cover the full student journey. An application submitted online becomes a student record, which then carries fee schedules, attendance, grades and communication history. Parents use a bilingual app to see notices, pay fees, sign permission forms and message teachers, while staff see everything in one place.

Fee collection was the feature administrators mentioned most. Schools want to offer instalment plans, apply sibling discounts, send automatic reminders and accept online payment, with every receipt recorded against the right student. Finance staff said reconciliation became much simpler once payments and invoices were generated by the same system, and that invoices must still meet the school's VAT and e-invoicing obligations.

Because these systems hold information about children, data protection is a serious consideration. Schools are reviewing where platforms host data, who among staff can see medical notes or family details, and how long records are kept after a student leaves, in line with the Personal Data Protection Law. Administrators recommend checking the latest guidance from the relevant education and data authorities.

title: Kuwaiti Landlords and Property Managers Move Rent Collection Online
subtitle: Property owners and management companies in Kuwait are adopting cloud property-management software to track leases, collect rent and handle maintenance requests.
excerpt: Investment buildings with dozens of units are moving from ledgers and cheques to platforms that remind tenants, record payments and log repairs in one place.
imageCaption: Looking up at glass office towers against the sky.
keyTakeaways: Lease tracking and automatic rent reminders are the main reasons Kuwaiti owners adopt property software.
Tenant portals for payments and maintenance requests reduce phone calls and disputes.
Owners should check that the software produces Arabic documents and exports cleanly to their accounting system.
content: Investment buildings are a common asset for Kuwaiti families and companies, and many are still run with paper ledgers, cheques and a building watchman's notebook. Property managers we spoke to said that model becomes difficult once an owner holds several buildings, and that more clients are now asking for cloud property-management software to bring leases, payments and maintenance together.

The core features are similar across products. Each unit and lease is recorded with rent amount, due dates and renewal terms. The system sends reminders to tenants before rent is due, records payments made by transfer or online link, and flags overdue accounts. Owners receive a statement per building showing income, arrears and expenses, which several described as the first time they had seen their portfolio clearly.

Tenant portals and apps are the second element. Tenants can pay rent, download receipts and log maintenance requests with photos, which are then assigned to a technician or contractor. Managers said this had reduced calls and arguments over whether a repair was reported, because every request has a timestamp and history. Owners can also see how quickly contractors respond and which units generate the most repair work.

Before choosing a platform, managers recommend checking that lease documents and notices can be produced in Arabic, that the system handles the payment methods tenants actually use, and that data exports cleanly to the owner's accounting software. Tenant personal details and identity documents also need secure storage, with access limited to the staff who need them.

title: Saudisation Targets Push HR Software Towards Built-In Nitaqat Tracking
subtitle: Saudi employers want their HR platforms to show where they stand on Saudisation in real time, and are asking vendors how well their systems reflect the Nitaqat rules.
excerpt: Keeping track of Saudisation status has become a routine management task. HR software that models headcount against Nitaqat bands is now a common requirement in Saudi tenders.
imageCaption: An aerial daytime view of the Riyadh skyline with the Kingdom Centre tower under a blue sky.
keyTakeaways: Employers want HR dashboards that show their Saudisation position before official figures update.
Rules on how employees are counted vary by activity and change over time, so software must be kept current.
Official platforms remain the source of truth, and HR software should be reconciled against them regularly.
content: Saudisation is a central part of workforce policy in the Kingdom. Under the Nitaqat programme, private-sector employers are placed in bands according to the share of Saudi nationals in their workforce, with requirements varying by economic activity and company size. The band affects what a company can do, including some visa and government service requests, so HR teams watch it closely.

HR directors we spoke to said they no longer want to discover their position only when the official figure changes. They want their HR platform to show the current ratio and to model what would happen if a planned hire, resignation or transfer went ahead. That requirement now appears regularly in Saudi tenders for HR and payroll software.

subheadings.title: Why the detail matters
paragraphs: The difficulty is that Nitaqat calculations depend on detailed rules about which employees count, how certain categories are weighted, and which activity code applies to each entity. Those rules have been updated several times over the years. HR leaders said they ask vendors how their calculation is built, who maintains it, and how quickly it is updated when the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development changes the rules. Groups with several commercial registrations face added complexity, since each entity may sit in a different activity and band.

subheadings.title: A planning tool, not the official record
paragraphs: Every HR director we spoke to was clear that the official government platforms remain the source of truth. Software dashboards are used for planning and early warning, and figures are reconciled with official records each month. Employers are advised to treat any vendor's Nitaqat feature as an estimate, to keep employee nationality and contract data clean, and to check the Ministry's latest guidance whenever rules change.

title: Oman's E-Invoicing Plans: What Accounting Software Buyers Should Check
subtitle: With Oman's Tax Authority working towards electronic invoicing, Omani businesses buying or renewing accounting software are asking vendors how they intend to support it.
excerpt: Details and timelines are for the Tax Authority to confirm, but Omani finance teams say it is sensible to choose software with a credible e-invoicing roadmap and clean VAT data now.
imageCaption: Earth at night seen from orbit, with city lights visible.
keyTakeaways: Oman's Tax Authority has signalled plans for e-invoicing, and businesses should follow its official announcements for scope and timing.
Clean customer and supplier tax data is useful preparation whatever the final requirements.
Buyers should ask vendors about their e-invoicing plans for Oman and their record in other GCC mandates.
content: Oman introduced VAT at 5 per cent in 2021, and its Tax Authority has signalled plans to move towards electronic invoicing, following a path already taken in Saudi Arabia and under way in the UAE. Finance managers we spoke to in Muscat said that, although the detailed requirements and timing are for the Authority to confirm, the direction is clear enough to affect software decisions being made now.

The practical effect is on procurement. Companies buying a new accounting or ERP system, or renewing an existing one, are adding questions about e-invoicing to their evaluations. They want to know whether the vendor plans to support Oman's requirements once published, how it has handled e-invoicing in other GCC countries, and whether compliance would come as a standard update or a paid add-on.

Advisers stress that the most useful preparation does not depend on final details. E-invoicing systems typically require accurate tax registration numbers for customers and suppliers, consistent product and service descriptions, correct VAT treatment on every line and a reliable invoice numbering sequence. Businesses that clean this data now will find any future transition easier, and will also file more accurate VAT returns in the meantime.

Advisers also caution against buying add-ons or connectors marketed as Oman e-invoicing solutions before official specifications are confirmed. They recommend that businesses follow the Tax Authority's official announcements, keep their accountants and software partners informed, and treat claims of early compliance with care until the requirements are formally published. Choosing a vendor with a clear update policy matters more today than any early feature.

title: E-Signatures Across the GCC: What Contract Software Buyers Should Know
subtitle: Electronic signature and contract-management tools are now common in Gulf businesses, but the legal framework differs by country and by type of document.
excerpt: Every GCC state recognises electronic signatures in some form. Legal and procurement teams say the details, including exceptions and trust-service rules, should shape how contract software is configured.
imageCaption: A hand holding a phone calculator over printed invoices.
keyTakeaways: GCC countries have electronic transactions laws that recognise electronic signatures, with conditions and exceptions.
Some documents may require a higher level of signature or traditional formalities, so templates should be reviewed by counsel.
Arabic signing flows and clear audit trails are practical requirements for regional deployments.
content: Electronic signature and contract-management software has moved from a convenience to a standard tool in many Gulf businesses, used for employment contracts, supplier agreements, sales orders and internal approvals. Legal and procurement leads we spoke to across the region said the technology is mature, but that deploying it across several GCC countries requires more thought than buying a single global subscription.

Each GCC state has an electronic transactions law that gives legal effect to electronic signatures and records, subject to conditions. Several also define higher levels of electronic signature backed by licensed trust-service providers or national digital identity schemes. Some categories of document, often including certain property, family and notarised matters, may be excluded or need extra formalities.

subheadings.title: Matching signature type to document
paragraphs: Legal teams described a tiered approach. Routine commercial documents such as purchase orders and non-disclosure agreements are signed with a standard electronic signature and a full audit trail. Higher-value or more sensitive agreements may use a stronger signature linked to national identity where available. Documents that require notarisation or registration follow the relevant official process. Counsel review which tier applies to each template before the software is configured.

subheadings.title: Practical requirements for Gulf deployments
paragraphs: Beyond the law, buyers said Arabic support is essential. Signers should see instructions in Arabic, documents should render right-to-left correctly, and audit certificates should be readable by Arabic-speaking reviewers. Procurement teams also ask where signed documents are stored, how long the vendor keeps them, and how they can be exported. Because legal details vary and change, teams are advised to take local legal advice for each country.

title: Emiratisation Targets Shape What UAE Employers Want From HR Software
subtitle: Private-sector employers in the UAE are asking HR platforms to track Emirati headcount, pension registration and target progress alongside the usual payroll and leave features.
excerpt: As Emiratisation requirements have widened, HR and payroll software in the UAE is expected to show employers where they stand and to keep the supporting records in order.
imageCaption: Dubai skyscrapers at dusk, with light trails on Sheikh Zayed Road.
keyTakeaways: Employers want a live view of Emirati headcount against the targets that apply to their company.
Accurate records of contracts, salaries and pension registration support any compliance review.
Global HR platforms often rely on local partners or configuration for UAE-specific requirements.
content: Emiratisation has become a regular agenda item for HR leaders across the UAE private sector. Targets for employing UAE nationals apply to companies above certain size thresholds and, in some cases, to smaller companies in specified sectors, under rules set by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. HR directors we spoke to in Dubai and Abu Dhabi said tracking progress has become a monthly task rather than an annual one.

That has changed what they ask of HR software. Beyond payroll, leave and end-of-service calculations, employers want dashboards showing Emirati headcount by entity, how it compares with the applicable target, and how planned hires or departures would affect the position. They also want the platform to hold the supporting evidence: contracts, salary records and pension registration for UAE national employees.

Pension contributions are a particular area of care for payroll teams, since UAE national employees must be registered with the relevant pension authority and contributions calculated correctly. HR managers said they test how platforms handle these calculations during evaluations, including for staff whose salary changes mid-month, and check that payroll exports match what is filed with the pension authority.

Employers using global HR platforms said UAE-specific features are sometimes handled through local partners or custom configuration rather than built into the core product. Advisers recommend confirming how each requirement is met before signing, keeping official ministry records as the reference point, and checking the latest guidance whenever targets or rules are updated. HR leaders said vendors that publish clear release notes for UAE changes earn more trust.

title: UAE IT Teams Add SaaS Backup and Data Export to Their Resilience Plans
subtitle: Companies that moved core systems to SaaS are realising that the vendor's own resilience does not cover every scenario, and are planning their own backups and exit routes.
excerpt: Accidental deletion, a compromised account or a decision to switch vendors can all leave a business needing its data back. UAE IT managers are putting backup and export plans in place before they need them.
imageCaption: Server racks with network cabling.
keyTakeaways: SaaS vendors protect their platforms, but customers are usually responsible for recovering from their own users' mistakes.
Regular exports or third-party backups of critical SaaS data are becoming standard practice.
Contracts should state how and in what format data can be retrieved at the end of a subscription.
content: Many UAE companies now run their CRM, accounting, HR and collaboration tools entirely as SaaS. IT managers we spoke to in Dubai said a common assumption was that moving to the cloud also solved backup, because the vendor runs resilient infrastructure. Several have since found that the vendor's protection is designed to keep the platform running, not to restore a single customer's deleted records from three weeks ago.

Most SaaS contracts describe this as a shared responsibility. The vendor keeps the service available and protects its infrastructure, while the customer is responsible for how its own users and integrations handle data. Retention windows for deleted items, version history and restore options differ from product to product. IT managers said they had rarely read those sections of the terms closely until something went wrong and they needed a record back quickly.

subheadings.title: The scenarios that prompt action
paragraphs: The situations managers described were rarely dramatic. A user bulk-deletes contacts by mistake. An integration overwrites fields across thousands of records. An employee leaves and their files disappear with their account. A compromised login is used to alter data. In each case, the vendor's ability to help depends on its retention settings and support terms, which vary widely between products and plan levels. Some teams discovered that the restore options they assumed were included applied only to higher-priced plans.

subheadings.title: What companies are putting in place
paragraphs: The response has two parts. First, regular backups of the most critical SaaS data, either through scheduled exports or a third-party backup service that copies records to separate storage. Teams then test restores, since a backup that cannot be restored is of little use. Where backups contain personal data, managers check where the copies are stored and who can access them.

Second, companies are reviewing exit terms. They want contracts to state that data can be exported in a usable, documented format, including attachments and history, within a defined period after cancellation. IT leaders said testing a full export once a year also shows how dependent they are on any single vendor, and how long a migration would realistically take.

title: Qatari Companies Bring Their SaaS Apps Behind Single Sign-On
subtitle: IT teams in Doha are connecting CRM, HR, finance and collaboration apps to a central identity provider so that access can be granted and removed in one place.
excerpt: With dozens of SaaS subscriptions in use, Qatari organisations are using single sign-on to cut password sprawl and make sure leavers lose access everywhere on their last day.
imageCaption: Server racks with network cabling.
keyTakeaways: Single sign-on lets IT teams enforce strong authentication and remove access from all connected apps at once.
Some SaaS products only offer SSO on higher-priced plans, which affects licence budgets.
Apps that cannot be connected to SSO need a separate, documented process for joiners and leavers.
content: Mid-sized organisations in Qatar typically use dozens of SaaS applications, each with its own login. IT managers we spoke to in Doha said that sprawl creates two problems. Staff reuse weak passwords across apps, and when someone leaves, removing every account depends on IT knowing every app that person used. Several described finding active accounts belonging to staff who had left months earlier.

Single sign-on addresses both. Applications are connected to a central identity provider, so staff log in once with their company account, protected by multi-factor authentication. When an employee leaves and their central account is disabled, access to every connected app ends at the same time. Some setups also create and remove accounts in connected apps automatically as staff join or change roles.

Cost is a common obstacle. Some SaaS vendors offer SSO only on their higher-priced plans, so connecting an app can mean upgrading every licence. IT managers said they prioritise apps holding financial, customer or HR data, and negotiate on the rest at renewal. Procurement teams are now adding SSO support to their standard requirements for new software.

Not every app can be connected, especially smaller niche tools. For those, IT teams keep a register of owners and users and add them to formal joiner and leaver checklists. Advisers also recommend reviewing access to sensitive apps every quarter, since role changes within the company can leave people with permissions they no longer need.

title: Bahraini Finance Teams Tighten User Roles and Audit Logs in Accounting Software
subtitle: Finance managers in Manama are reviewing who can approve, edit and delete transactions in their cloud accounting and ERP systems, and checking that every change leaves a trace.
excerpt: Shared logins and broad administrator rights were common when teams first moved to cloud accounting. Bahraini finance leaders are now setting role-based permissions and using audit logs as a routine control.
imageCaption: A laptop showing a sales analytics dashboard on a desk.
keyTakeaways: Each user should have an individual login with permissions matched to their role.
Separating who creates, approves and pays transactions reduces the risk of error and fraud.
Audit logs are only useful if someone reviews them regularly.
content: When many Bahraini SMEs first moved to cloud accounting, convenience came first. Finance managers we spoke to in Manama admitted that shared logins, a single administrator account used by several people, and broad rights for everyone were common. As businesses have grown and auditors have asked more questions, those habits are being replaced by role-based permissions and regular use of audit logs.

The starting point is individual accounts. Every person who uses the system gets their own login, protected by multi-factor authentication, so every action can be traced to a named user. Roles are then set according to job: a clerk can enter bills but not approve them, an approver can approve but not change bank details, and only a small number of senior staff hold administrator rights.

Separation of duties is the principle behind those roles. Finance managers said the most important split is between the person who sets up or edits a supplier's bank details and the person who releases payments. Most cloud accounting and ERP platforms support approval workflows and restrictions of this kind, but they need to be configured deliberately and reviewed when staff change roles.

Audit logs record who created, edited or deleted each transaction and when. Managers said they now review logs as part of month-end close, looking at deleted invoices, changes to closed periods and edits to supplier details. External auditors increasingly ask for evidence of that review, and businesses should check how long their platform keeps log history.

title: Gulf SaaS Startups Learn to Answer Enterprise Security Questionnaires
subtitle: Young software companies selling to banks, government-linked entities and large groups across the GCC are finding that security reviews can decide a deal as much as product features.
excerpt: Long security questionnaires have become a routine step in enterprise SaaS sales in the Gulf. Founders say preparing standard answers and evidence early shortens sales cycles considerably.
imageCaption: Earth at night seen from orbit, with city lights visible.
keyTakeaways: Enterprise buyers in the GCC routinely send detailed security questionnaires before signing with a SaaS vendor.
Questions on data residency, local data protection laws and sector regulator requirements are now standard.
A maintained library of answers and supporting documents helps startups respond quickly and consistently.
content: For a GCC software startup, winning its first large enterprise customer often brings a new kind of paperwork. Founders we spoke to in Riyadh, Dubai and Manama described receiving security questionnaires running to hundreds of questions from banks, insurers, government-linked entities and large family groups. Several said a deal had stalled for weeks while they worked out how to answer.

The questionnaires cover familiar ground: access control, encryption, backups, incident response, staff vetting and software development practices. Increasingly, they also ask region-specific questions, including where customer data is hosted, how the vendor complies with national data protection laws such as Saudi Arabia's PDPL, and whether it can meet the outsourcing expectations of the buyer's sector regulator.

subheadings.title: Building a reusable answer library
paragraphs: Founders who now handle these reviews smoothly described a common approach. They keep a single, maintained library of approved answers, reviewed by whoever owns security, along with supporting documents such as policies, architecture diagrams, penetration test summaries and incident response plans. Each new questionnaire is answered from that library, and new questions are added as they appear, so answers stay consistent across customers. Some also publish a short security overview that sales teams can share before a formal questionnaire arrives.

subheadings.title: Being honest about gaps
paragraphs: Startups rarely have every control a large enterprise expects. Founders and the security advisers who work with them said buyers respond better to clear answers about what is in place, what is planned and by when, than to vague claims. Formal certifications help but take time and money, so many startups prioritise the controls their target customers ask about most. Promises made in questionnaires often become contract terms, so they must be accurate.
